svg.title: The Political Insanity Loop — From Public Opinion to Civic Agency
svg.desc: A repository edition of the Political Insanity Loop. The large left-to-right diagnostic map tests recurring political responses to social harm and preserves useful components while tracing the invariant failure of nonbinding public opinion toward the proposed functions of correctable civic agency in A Universal Union.
svg.text: A UNIVERSAL UNION · CIVIC AGENCY DIAGNOSTIC
From repeated political failure to the missing functions of correctable public power.

g.text: RUN EVERY PROPOSED SOLUTION INSIDE A MODEL OF REALITY
OBSERVATION + HISTORY CAN TEST AN IDEA BEFORE YOU LIVE IT
for it · unsure · persuadable · against it
Popularity is evidence—not permission to ignore everyone else.
A small organized veto can beat a large scattered majority.
ballot · persuasion · pressure · parallel build · revolt
A goal is not a plan for reaching or surviving power.
WHAT HAPPENS TO PEOPLE WHO SAY NO?
speak · appeal · opt out locally · build alternatives
Disagreement needs protection—but cannot excuse harming others.
who sets the agenda · acts · records · corrects?
A solution fails if success merely creates the next ruler.
THE INVARIANT: POWER “WON’T LISTEN” WHILE PUBLIC OPINION REMAINS ADVICE RATHER THAN BINDING, CORRECTABLE ACTION.
People enter this map at different places. The left-to-right spine shows what repeated failure makes visible.
observe → feel pain → become angry → blame
bad outcomes look like bad leadership
maybe the menu, voters, incentives, or electoral rules are broken
TRY TO MAKE REPRESENTATION MORE ACCURATE.
truth, numbers, disruption, leverage, or force
04 · MAYBE THE WHOLE SYSTEM IS WRONG
change ownership · state · scale · organizing doctrine
TRY A DIFFERENT ANSWER FOR EVERYONE.
vote on issues · deliberate · delegate · build locally
not the perfect ruler—the ability to rule together
PUBLIC POWER MUST ALSO BE CORRECTABLE.
the mind looks for a cause
a visible ruler is easier to see
Failure becomes useful only when the mind asks:
If bad people cause bad outcomes,
THIS IS THE FIRST SOLUTION TO TEST.
before it points toward a system.
Next: does a new ruler change the outcome?
A new occupant inherits the same office,
party, donors, bureaucracy, and legal limits.
The public swaps one bundled program
The outsider meets the same institutions—
or tries to concentrate power personally.
Neither replaces audit, appeal, or recall.
A coup, assassination, or revolt removes
the occupant faster than an election.
The strongest faction inherits the machine.
Next guess: perhaps the selection process is broken.
Power can still ignore the signal.
Policy is bargained after the vote.
The same state enforces the rules.
Courts act later; access is unequal.
THE HARDEST CASE: FUNCTIONING REPRESENTATIVE DEMOCRACIES
A PARTY CAN PROMISE A POPULAR POLICY, WIN,
THEN DELAY, DILUTE, ABANDON, OR IGNORE IT.
A victory controls only some nodes.
Elections authorize officeholders, not enforceable issue mandates.
Next attempt: pressure officeholders until they respond.
can make reality visible. Power can ignore it.
Officeholders decide whether the request counts.
A peaceful occupation made grievance visible
without creating a public mandate or implementation path.
Participants may not represent every affected person.
Force challenges an outcome without a legitimate
public process for authorizing a successor.
Courts can restrain power after harm.
They are reactive and unequal to access.
It does not make the public sovereign.
Next conclusion: perhaps the system itself must be replaced.
Winning office does not control investment,
Still unanswered: what happens to people
who reject the new economic system?
It does not answer who actually governs:
The old system will not surrender easily.
The transition centralizes power to survive.
A new system can still silence dissent.
Removing the state removes one hierarchy.
KEEP: exit where people can leave.
Power moves closer to affected people.
Local elites and internal minorities remain.
KEEP: LOCAL POWER FOR LOCAL NEEDS.
The answer creates one distant institution
valuable enough for everyone to capture.
A new universal system still needs a way
to live with people who reject it.
Next question: can people keep decision-making power themselves?
A small group studies one issue.
One person may block the rest—
Good people still disagree, forget, and make mistakes.
KEEP: HUMILITY + EDUCATION + A CULTURE OF PARTICIPATION.
Goodness is not a governance protocol.
These are pieces of the answer—
not yet a shared civic operating system.
The missing problem is now visible.
They may speak, vote, protest, strike, and revolt—
yet remain downstream of organized power.
not wait for a party to place it on the agenda
supporters · opponents · people bearing the cost
revise the proposal before forcing a false choice
who may do what · where · for how long
expertise can serve without owning authority
local autonomy + coordination across shared problems
A CORRECTABLE WAY TO RULE TOGETHER.
No institution becomes the only court allowed
WHAT SURVIVES THE TEST · AUU DOES NOT THROW EVERY EARLIER IDEA AWAY
Each failed “complete solution” contributes a requirement for a more complete civic system.
People must be able to end authority
Different views need room to organize
Speech must connect to peaceful capacity
Different models can coexist where consequences
remain local and shared rights remain protected.
People need power before, during, and after
Local power must coordinate without being
THE ROOT PROBLEM IS NOT “WHICH ANSWER SHOULD RULE EVERYONE?”
IT IS: “HOW CAN AFFECTED PEOPLE BUILD, AUTHORIZE, AND CORRECT ANSWERS TOGETHER?”
THE END OF THE LOOP IS NOT CERTAINTY. IT IS CORRECTABLE COLLECTIVE AGENCY.

svg.text: CONCEPTUAL MAP · REQUIREMENTS, NOT A CLAIM OF IMPLEMENTATION
